facts.raw_span: A 65-year-old man
hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and bronchial asthma
mild headaches of several months’ duration
no focal neurologic deficits
cranial MRI 4 years earlier for unrelated reasons, with no significant change in the identified lesion since then
Laboratory studies were normal
Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a well-defined, 19-mm mass in the left parietal bone near the squamosal suture
centred in the diploic space, with sparse but preserved trabeculae and a slight bony bulge, without disruption of the inner or outer tables
MRI showed the lesion to be isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images
with multiple internal hyperintense foci, heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images, and restricted diffusion
the hyperintense foci on T1 images were presumed to represent bone marrow fat
the preserved trabecular architecture suggested that pre-existing structures were not destroyed

concepts.why: The well-defined, 19-mm mass in the left parietal bone near the squamosal suture, centred in the diploic space, with sparse but preserved trabeculae and a slight bony bulge, is consistent with a diploic space osteoma, which is supported by the MRI findings of isointensity to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images.

The presence of a well-defined mass in the diploic space with preserved trabeculae and a slight bony bulge, along with the MRI findings of isointensity to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images, could also suggest a hemangioma of the skull, which is known to have a similar appearance on imaging studies.

The imaging findings of a well-defined mass in the diploic space with sparse but preserved trabeculae and a slight bony bulge could also be consistent with fibrous dysplasia of the skull, which can present with a similar appearance on CT and MRI studies.
